blocks.text: SCHNURRER, in his Dissertat. in Esaj. XXVII. (in his collected Dissertations, p. 323 ff.), following ED. POCOCK in his Comment. ad Mich. I, 8., holds that two names must be distinguished, similar indeed, but nonetheless truly different. The one is תן, the jackal, or wild dog [which among the Hebrews is called by other names, אי and שועל; see above vol. 1, book 3, Chapter 12, 13]; it does not occur in the singular in the surviving Hebrew literature, and has a plural of several forms, תנים, תנין and תנות. The other is תנין, for which in Ezekiel תנים occurs twice, perhaps only through the carelessness of copyists; its plural is תנינים, and it means dragon and things similar to it. This is confirmed not only by the authority and agreement of the Arabic dialect, in which تِنّينٌ [tinnīn] is dragon, great serpent, while تِينان [tīnān] is wolf, which is closely related to that wild dog, but also by R. Tanchum, a Jew of Jerusalem and a most excellent commentator, who in his Arabic commentary, a copy of which exists in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, in several places (on Mich. I, 8. Ierem. IX, 10. Thren. IV, 3. Malach. I, 3.) denies that the meaning dragon can apply, and teaches that the animal called ابن اوي [ibn awī], ibn awi, or ابن واوي [ibn wāwī], ibn wawi, is to be understood. To this is added the authority of the Syriac translator of the Old Testament, who uses now a word agreeing with the Hebrew, ܬܢܝܢܐ, now another name, ܝܪܘܪܐ, meaning wild dog or jackal. Nor does the Syriac translator use these words indiscriminately and at random, but in such a way that he is readily seen to have kept a fixed and consistent rule. For he employs the word ܝܪܘܪܐ wherever the Hebrew text has the plural תנים, or תנין, or תנות, with the single exception of Ps. XLIV, 20. Conversely, whenever תנין occurs in the singular (to which the form תנים, used twice by Ezekiel, XXIX, 3. and XXXII, 3., also belongs), or its plural, [III, 223] תנינים, the Syriac too uses the name that corresponds exactly to it, ܬܢܝܢܐ. The Chaldee version agrees with the Syriac in this way: where the latter uses the word ܝܪܘܪܐ, the former puts ירורא, which was indeed usually taken in the sense of dragon, but plainly arose from the confusion of the similar letters ד and ר, and so is to be restored to ירודא and taken in the same sense which, as POCOCK attests, the Syriac writers themselves give to the word ܝܪܘܪܐ, namely jackal. [But what if the confusion of the letters ? and ; occurred in the Syriac version, so that, on the evidence of the Chaldee version, which consistently has ירודא, ܝܪܘܕܐ should be restored for ܝܪܘܪܐ?] CHR. TH. TYCHSEN agrees with Schnurrer on MICHAELIS, Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2371, except that he thinks תנות in Mal. I, 3. should be referred to the root تنا [tanā], he stayed, whence تناة [tanāh], dwelling, and translated so, following the Alexandrians and the Syriac. — For OEDMANN, in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 4, ch. 4, תנין, תנים and תנות is the Hippopotamus Amphibius Linn., because what is attributed to the תנין in the Old Testament fits this animal very well, such as its immense size (Ps. CXLVIII, 7.), its dwelling in the waters (Es. XXVII, 1. LI, 9.), its bellowing (Mich. I, 8.). Moreover, that in Thren. IV, 3. the תנין are said to give the breast to their young, and that in Ierem. XIV, 6. Ps. LXXIV, 13. their heads are described as standing above the waters to catch the air, suits the hippopotamus best. Although this view has something to commend it at first sight, it is entirely without the support of the other dialects cognate with Hebrew and of the agreement of the ancient translators. To me, from the primary meaning of the verb تنّ [tanna], which the Arab lexicographers, as ALB. SCHULTENS reports in his Comment. ad Iob. XL, 20, p. 1170, explain by the synonym قصع [qaṣaʿa], that is, to swallow, to swallow down, with jaws wide open, تنين [tinnīn] and תנין seem to embrace any terrible beasts of immense size, aquatic as well as terrestrial (a meaning most fitting in Ies. XXXIV, 13. Ierem. IX, 10.), yet so that it is sometimes also used of certain particular huge and harmful beasts, such as serpents, Exod. VII, 9. compared with IV, 3. VII, 15., the crocodile, Ps. LXXIV, 13.14. Esaj. XXVII, 1., in which places תנין and לויתן are used interchangeably, and sea monsters, Genes. I, 21. Ps. CIV, 26. CXLVIII, 7.
That this is to be referred to the Boa constrictor Linn. (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 3, p. 1083, 13th ed.) is Schneider's probable conjecture on this passage of Aelian.
